title: Vector triangles for coplanar equilibrium
prior_knowledge_summary: A system is in equilibrium only when its resultant force is zero and its resultant torque is zero.
Force balance and moment balance are separate checks.
A moment is calculated from force and perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Coplanar vectors can be added head-to-tail and resolved into perpendicular components.
new_learning: Three coplanar forces on an object in equilibrium form a closed head-to-tail vector triangle.
Each side of an equilibrium triangle must preserve the magnitude and direction of its force.
An unknown equilibrium force can be found from triangle geometry or from perpendicular component balance.
A closed force triangle proves zero resultant force, but rotational equilibrium must still be checked separately for a rigid body.

learning_outcomes.text: understand that, when there is no resultant force and no resultant torque, a system is in equilibrium
use a vector triangle to represent coplanar forces in equilibrium

visual_planning.reason: Six planned figures distribute the visual teaching across closure, direction preservation, geometry, component balance, a rigid-body check and synthesis. Asset generation is outside this deterministic four-file package.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why does the last arrow return to the start?
content: A small ring is pulled by three ropes and stays exactly where it is. One rope pulls east, one pulls north and the third pulls down and left.
Draw the three force arrows head-to-tail. If the ring is in equilibrium, the last arrow lands exactly at the starting point. The arrows make a closed triangle.
That closure is not a drawing trick. It is a visible statement that the three force vectors add to zero.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a closed force triangle by linking a stationary ring to a head-to-tail loop.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper teacher sketch. Left panel shows a ring with three differently directed force arrows. Right panel slides the same three arrows head-to-tail into a closed triangle. Keep force labels as A, B and C and show no numerical values.
figure.alt_text: Three forces acting on a ring are rearranged head-to-tail to form a closed triangle.

blocks.title: Closure is the force condition written as a picture
content: A force is a vector, so both its size and direction matter. When force A is followed by force B and then force C, the final point shows the combined effect of all three forces.

For equilibrium, the resultant force is zero. The final point must therefore be the same as the starting point. This gives the vector statement $\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}=\vec{0}$ and the graphical statement that the force polygon closes.

With exactly three non-parallel coplanar forces, the closed polygon is a triangle. Draw arrows continuously head-to-tail. A side may be moved parallel to itself, but it must not be rotated, reversed or stretched unless its force direction or scale requires that change.
The order of the three sides may change. The triangle still closes if every force keeps its own magnitude and direction.

figure.purpose: Show how head-to-tail closure represents a zero vector sum and distinguish a valid reordered triangle from an invalid reversed force.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper comparison. Show two valid closed triangles using the same three directed arrows in different cyclic orders. Beside them show one open chain caused by reversing one arrow, marked as the error. Use sparse labels and no values.
figure.alt_text: Two differently ordered force triangles close, while a chain with one reversed force does not.

blocks.title: Find the balancing force by triangle geometry
content: Consider a ring pulled by 36 N east and 48 N north. A third force keeps the ring in equilibrium.
Place the 48 N north arrow at the head of the 36 N east arrow. These perpendicular forces have a combined effect of $\sqrt{36^2+48^2}=60$ N towards the north-east.
The balancing force must close the triangle. It runs from the final head back to the original tail, so it has magnitude 60 N and points south-west.
Its direction is $\tan^{-1}(48/36)=53.1^\circ$ south of west. This is the opposite direction to the resultant of the first two forces.
Independent check: a right-triangle hypotenuse must be longer than 48 N but shorter than $36+48=84$ N. The value 60 N passes this check.

figure.purpose: Model a complete geometry route from two perpendicular forces to the third balancing force.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper worked layout. Draw 36 N east followed by 48 N north, then a 60 N closing arrow back to the start. Mark 53.1 degrees south of west at the appropriate corner. Add a small magnitude bound check. Keep all arrow directions exact.
figure.alt_text: A 36 newton east force and a 48 newton north force are closed by a 60 newton force directed 53.1 degrees south of west.

blocks.title: Components give the same closure without a scale drawing
content: A closed triangle means that horizontal components cancel and vertical components cancel. Choose positive directions before writing any component values.

Suppose force A is 50 N east and force B is 80 N at $60^\circ$ north of west. With east and north positive, B has horizontal component $-80\cos60^\circ=-40$ N and vertical component $+80\sin60^\circ=+69.3$ N.
The first two forces therefore combine to $+10$ N east and $+69.3$ N north. The third force must provide exactly the opposite components: 10 N west and 69.3 N south.
Its magnitude is $\sqrt{10^2+69.3^2}=70.0$ N. Its direction is $\tan^{-1}(10/69.3)=8.21^\circ$ west of south.
Independent check: adding the third force gives zero in each direction. This component check is the numerical version of seeing the triangle close.

figure.purpose: Connect a closed force triangle to signed horizontal and vertical component cancellation.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper split layout. Left shows the three-force triangle for 50 N east, 80 N at 60 degrees north of west and the unknown closing force. Right shows a two-row component table whose totals become zero after the closing force is included. Use exact signs and units.
figure.alt_text: A force triangle and a signed component table both show horizontal and vertical totals of zero.

blocks.title: A closed force triangle does not by itself prove full equilibrium
content: It is tempting to see a closed force triangle and conclude that every object must be in equilibrium. Closure proves only that the resultant force is zero.
A rigid body can still have a non-zero resultant torque. For example, equal opposite forces on different lines of action have zero resultant force but form a couple, so the body can rotate.
The previous lesson supplied the complete test: zero resultant force and zero resultant torque. Use a vector triangle for the force test and a moment calculation for the torque test.
For a particle-sized junction where all three lines of action meet at one point, the force triangle is normally the main check. For an extended rigid body, keep the torque check separate.

figure.purpose: Contrast zero force with full equilibrium by showing a force-balanced pair that still produces rotation.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper comparison. Left shows a small junction with three concurrent forces and a closed triangle. Right shows a horizontal bar with equal opposite parallel forces on separate lines of action, zero force sum and a curved rotation arrow. Label the two checks as force and torque only.
figure.alt_text: A closed triangle gives zero resultant force, while separated equal opposite forces can still turn a rigid body.

blocks.title: Use moments first, then close the force triangle
content: A horizontal beam of length 1.2 m is hinged at one end. Its 240 N weight acts at the midpoint. A cable at the far end pulls at $30^\circ$ above the beam.

Take moments about the hinge. Using the controlled relationship $M=Fd_\perp$, the weight moment is $240\times0.60=144$ N m. The cable's vertical component gives the opposing moment: $(T\sin30^\circ)\times1.2$.
Equating the moments gives $(T\sin30^\circ)\times1.2=144$, so $T=240$ N.
Now the beam has three forces: its weight, the cable tension and the hinge reaction. Place the known weight and tension head-to-tail. The hinge reaction is the closing side.

The tension components are 208 N left and 120 N up. After the 240 N downward weight, the closing reaction must be 208 N right and 120 N up. Its magnitude is 240 N at $30.0^\circ$ above the horizontal.
Independent checks: the moment equation is satisfied, the horizontal components cancel and the vertical components cancel. Both equilibrium conditions now pass.

symbols_and_units.d_\\perp: perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action in m

figure.purpose: Show the stage boundary between rotational balance and the three-force vector triangle for one rigid body.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper two-stage worked sketch. Stage 1 shows a 1.2 m horizontal hinged beam, 240 N midpoint weight and cable at 30 degrees, with moment arms. Stage 2 shows the weight, 240 N tension and hinge reaction as a closed triangle. Include the final component cancellation check without decorative detail.
figure.alt_text: A beam problem is solved first by moments for cable tension and then by a closed force triangle for hinge reaction.

blocks.title: Close the loop, then check the turning effect
content: For three coplanar equilibrium forces, identify each force and its true direction. Place the arrows head-to-tail at one consistent scale. The third arrow must return to the start.
Use right-triangle geometry when the completed triangle is right-angled. Use signed horizontal and vertical components when that route is clearer. Both methods express the same zero vector sum.
Do not reverse a force just to make the picture close. The closing arrow's direction is fixed by the physical force it represents.
For an extended body, closure completes only the force test. Also confirm that the resultant torque is zero. Do not use Lami's theorem in this lesson.
